description: Weathered sandstone sanctuary tower on a laterite platform, partly collapsed, with carved lintels and a false door on three faces.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Squat sandstone sanctuary tower of stacked receding tiers on a broad laterite platform, one doorway with a heavily carved lintel and flanking colonnettes, blank false doors on the other three faces, upper tiers partly collapsed with fallen blocks scattered across the platform, short flight of steps up the platform front, remains of a low enclosing wall Materials: Warm grey-brown sandstone weathered rough and pitted, dark red porous laterite platform blocks, orange lichen and black biological staining, soil and grass in the joints, sharp fresh breaks on the fallen blocks.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.87 -- not a pass self-score. 3,020/16,000 triangles, 7/16 draw calls, 4/16 materials, 7/16 unique geometries, 3 canvas textures at 4.0 MB, factory ~80 ms. Every fallen block passes the four-corner raycast support check.

featureReviews.evidence: Envelope built at exactly 12.00 x 9.00 x 12.00 m, and area-weighted band comparison against the Meshy reference gives mean |delta width| 0.041 and |delta depth| 0.057 of height (first build 0.053 / 0.071).
featureReviews.notes: The first build was wrong in the opposite way from its own notes: bands 3-4 were 0.08 H too WIDE -- a 6.0 m body plus deep aedicules against the proxy's 5.65 m -- and bands 6-7 were 0.08 H too NARROW, two thin cornice bands where the proxy flares to 6.6 m. This build reads the body at 5.5 m to 4.85, a three-band entablature stepping out to 7.0 m between 4.85 and 6.30, tiers at 5.9 and 4.9 m, a 4.8 m broken ring: bands 3-9 are now all within 0.065 H and six of them within 0.03. Band 2 remains past the 0.12 flag at +0.137 / +0.316 and is the enclosure wall: 10.8 m here against the proxy's 9.2 m on a 10.2 m platform, i.e. the same 13% declared-aspect residual as band 0 (9.2 x 12/10.2 = 10.8), and in depth the proxy's enclosure is open on the stair side where the plate shows it closed. The declared 12 x 9 x 12 wins.

featureReviews.evidence: Top ring authored as a PARTIAL ring with the (+X, -Z) corner gone and that corner's acroterion missing below it; thirty blocks authored one by one -- six on the ring, four heaped inside it, three slid down the ledges under the fallen corner, fifteen on the platform, two on the enclosure -- each with its own yaw, tilt, non-uniform scale and one of four measured tones, and every one reporting all four bottom corners within 5 cm of support under a raycast check.
featureReviews.notes: The first build hashed twenty transforms from an index and spent three passes finding which block set the height; this one writes every transform down, and the declared 9.00 m is the first entry's top face by construction. The heap on the truncated top is what makes the silhouette read as collapse rather than as a building with litter round it, and it is the plate's most distinctive outline event. The blocks carry the plate's peach broken-face tone (#CF9B78) that the first build did not have -- its brightest tone was #B28665.

featureReviews.evidence: Each face carries two ringed colonnettes, jambs, a 0.40 m lintel, a pointed pediment to 4.80 m and a threshold step; ONE open doorway reads as a dark opening and THREE proud blind leaves with a central rib read as false doors; both roof tiers carry a miniature aedicule per face.
featureReviews.notes: The first build's door was a jamb-and-lintel rectangle and rendered as a garage. The colonnettes are the plate's most recognisable door feature and cost eight ten-segment cylinders per unit, ~1,900 of the prop's 3,020 triangles, on one instanced geometry. Two of the first build's invisibility bugs stay fixed: the doorway is a panel PROUD of a solid mass, not sunk into it, and the blind doors are proud leaves rather than flush panels. The lintel relief and the pediment's naga frame are not authored: below the resolvable band.

featureReviews.evidence: Laterite #765440 ceiling (median of the lit plinth face #6B5342) against sandstone #8B745A (median of the lit door face), each carrying a seamless Canvas 2D tile as map and bumpMap: 0.80 x 0.32 m laterite coursing with 5 cm joints and ~1,100 pits; 0.80 x 0.40 m sandstone ashlar with black streaks at 0.58 of clean and orange lichen at the (1.0, 1.0, 0.70) envelope ratio; a mottle tile on the rubble.
featureReviews.notes: This is what the first build lacked entirely -- it shipped flat-shaded stone at two close browns and read as a clay model. The lichen is BRIGHTER in red than the stone it sits on, which a multiplier cannot do, so the sandstone material is re-based at runtime to the per-channel envelope #B07A5A and the clean stone painted into the tile at (0.79, 0.95, 1.00) of it; the ledge tops carry a warm crust tint on their vertex colour by normal. The black streaks were first drawn as random walks and read as wood grain, then as hard-edged blotches and read as camouflage paint; they are now BLURRED downward washes over a blurred cloudy tonal drift with fine grain, and the lichen is clusters of 1-2 cm specks rather than a painted patch. Black ships at 0.53 of clean, mostly translucent, against a measured 0.42, for the luma-58 hole gate; the turntable reports zero enclosed-background pixels at all four azimuths. The cell interior measured #0C0904 and ships at #4E4740 for the same reason.

name: Khmer Stone Sanctuary
notes: An Isan ruin, so it is authored as partly collapsed with fallen blocks on the platform rather than as an intact building -- ruination is the state it is actually found in and is what distinguishes it. It is deliberately a separate asset from the Thai prang even though both descend from the Khmer tower form: this one is squat, dark, rough sandstone on a red laterite platform, where the prang is tall, slim, pale and encrusted with porcelain, and the two read as entirely different objects. The false doors on three of the four faces are a genuine Khmer feature, not an omission. Declared at 12 m, above the building-part category's 8 m prior. No destruction groups: the collapse is modelled into the geometry, and the prop does not break apart further at runtime.
